content: This publication is an updated version of the 2022 document titled “Guidelines for the Clinical Management of Severe Illness from Influenza Virus Infections.” It is available in both electronic (ISBN 978-92-4-009775-9) and print (ISBN 978-92-4-009776-6) formats. The World Health Organization (WHO) retains copyright for this 2024 edition, with some rights reserved under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO license. Users are permitted to copy, redistribute, and adapt the work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The document includes corrections made to the electronic file on September 17, 2024. For example, the dosage for children under 10 years was revised to a single 20 mg dose, and the duration of laninamivir inhalation therapy was adjusted from three days to two days. The guidelines aim to assist clinicians in managing patients with suspected or confirmed influenza virus infections. They provide recommendations for treating both severe and non-severe influenza, as well as for using antiviral medications to prevent infection in individuals exposed to the virus within the previous 48 hours. The scope of the guidelines has been expanded to include seasonal influenza viruses, pandemic influenza viruses, and novel influenza A viruses known to cause severe illness in humans, such as avian influenza A(H5N1), A(H5N6), and A(H7N9). Baseline risk estimates for hospitalization and death, derived from observational studies, are included, along with definitions of high-risk and extremely high-risk patients to better target recommendations. The target audience for these guidelines includes healthcare providers managing influenza patients at all levels of the healthcare system, from community-based care to hospital wards. The guidelines also serve as a reference for policymakers, health managers, and administrators in developing national, regional, and local guidelines for epidemic and pandemic preparedness. The executive summary outlines recommendations for antiviral treatment of both severe and non-severe influenza, adjunctive therapies for severe cases (e.g., corticosteroids, NSAIDs, macrolides, and passive immune therapy), diagnostic testing strategies, antiviral prophylaxis, and the use of concomitant antibiotics in non-severe cases. Key new recommendations include: A conditional recommendation for the use of baloxavir in non-severe influenza patients at high risk of progression to severe disease. A conditional recommendation against the use of baloxavir in non-severe influenza patients at low risk of severe disease progression. A conditional recommendation against the use of laninamivir for non-severe influenza. A strong recommendation against the use of oseltamivir for non-severe influenza. A conditional recommendation against the use of peramivir for non-severe influenza. A strong recommendation against the use of zanamivir for non-severe influenza. A strong recommendation against the use of favipiravir for non-severe influenza. A conditional recommendation against the use of umifenovir for non-severe influenza. A strong recommendation against the use of antibiotics in non-severe influenza patients with a low probability of bacterial co-infection. For severe influenza, including infections with novel influenza viruses, additional recommendations are provided, emphasizing the importance of evidence-based antiviral treatment strategies.
